about.title: Santa Clarita Medical Malpractice Claims
about.longDescription: Medical care in Santa Clarita reaches roughly 182,000 residents across Los Angeles County's northern valley, and most of it goes the way it should. When it doesn't — a delayed diagnosis, a surgical slip, a prescription that never should have been written — the aftermath can be confusing and expensive. California handles these claims under MICRA, a set of rules that differs from an ordinary injury case. You generally have one year from the date you discovered the harm, and never more than three years from the injury itself, to file. A 90-day notice must go to the provider before a lawsuit begins. Non-economic damages are capped, though that cap rises every year. And nearly every case needs a qualified medical expert to explain what a careful provider would have done differently. A disappointing result on its own is not malpractice; the question is whether the standard of care was breached. LawProactive is a free service that connects Santa Clarita residents with an independent attorney who handles these cases on contingency.

items.question: I was hurt in a crash on Sierra Highway and the emergency room missed a fracture. Is that a malpractice case or a car accident case?
items.answer: It may be both, and they are handled differently. Santa Clarita recorded 706 injury collisions in 2025, and a fair number of those patients later discover that a follow-up problem came from treatment rather than the crash itself. The auto claim runs on ordinary injury rules, while the missed-fracture claim falls under MICRA with its own deadlines and expert requirement. An attorney can sort out which is which and pursue each on its own track.

items.question: My surgery didn't go well. Does that mean I have a malpractice claim?
items.answer: Not necessarily. California law is clear that a bad outcome alone is not malpractice; the question is whether the provider fell below the standard of care a careful practitioner would have met. That usually requires a qualified medical expert to review your records and weigh in. An attorney can arrange that review and tell you honestly where things stand.

items.question: Is there a limit on what I can recover in a California medical malpractice case?
items.answer: MICRA caps non-economic damages — things like pain and loss of enjoyment of life — and that cap increases every year under current law. Economic losses such as medical bills and lost income are not subject to that cap. Every case is different, so an attorney can explain how these rules apply to your particular situation without anyone promising a result.
